Catalonia
kat-uh-LOH-nee-uh
n. (the principality of the crown of Aragon, whose Barcelona press printed early vernacular Scripture and whose liberties were broken in 1714)
From medieval Latin Catalaunia, of disputed origin, perhaps from the castellans of the Frankish march.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Catalonia is the north-eastern principality of the Spanish crowns, with its own language, its own law and, until 1714, its own institutions: the Corts, the Generalitat and the constitutions which the king swore to observe. Barcelona was an early printing centre, and a Catalan Bible was among the earliest vernacular Scriptures printed anywhere in Europe, the Valencian Bible of 1478, which the Inquisition suppressed so thoroughly that only a single leaf survives. Catalonia revolted in 1640 and again took the losing side in the war of the Spanish Succession, after which Philip the Fifth abolished its constitutions in 1714 and its universities, and prohibited official use of the language. The dictionary records Catalonia for the lost Bible. One printed leaf is all that remains of a vernacular Scripture that existed before Luther was born, which is the most compact evidence available that the desire for the Bible in the people's tongue was not a Protestant novelty but a Christian instinct that Rome had to work hard to suppress.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines vernacular as native to a country; to suppress as to put down or conceal; a leaf as a part of a book; a constitution as the established form of government; and translation as rendering into another language.

expand to see more

VERNACULAR, a. Native; belonging to the country of one's birth; as one's vernacular tongue.

SUPPRESS, v.t. To crush; to subdue; to destroy; to conceal; to keep in; to restrain from utterance or vent.

LEAF, n. A part of a book containing two pages; the thin, extended part of a plant.

CONSTITUTION, n. The established form of government in a state; the fundamental rules and principles by which a nation is governed.

TRANSLATION, n. The act of turning into another language; that which is produced by turning into another language.

Key Scripture

Psa 119:130 — "The entrance of thy words giveth light; it giveth understanding unto the simple."

Act 17:11 — "These were more noble than those in Thessalonica, in that they received the word with all readiness of mind, and searched the scriptures daily, whether those things were so."

Isa 55:11 — "So shall my word be that goeth forth out of my mouth: it shall not return unto me void, but it shall accomplish that which I please, and it shall prosper in the thing whereto I sent it."

Modern Corruption

North-eastern Spanish principality whose 1478 Valencian Bible survives in a single leaf, and whose constitutions were abolished in 1714.

expand to see more

The corruption to name is the suppression of vernacular Scripture, and Catalonia supplies the hardest piece of evidence for it, because the suppression was so complete that almost nothing is left to argue over. A Bible existed in the people's language in 1478 and was destroyed by a church that claimed to be its guardian. The reason given was the danger of private reading, and the Scriptures answer it with a commendation of exactly that practice: the Bereans “searched the scriptures daily, whether those things were so” (Act 17:11).

The second paragraph names the principle to recover. The text is designed to be understood by the unlearned, which is the whole argument for translation: “The entrance of thy words giveth light; it giveth understanding unto the simple” (Psa 119:130). God binds the effect of his word to his own sending and not to an authorisation, so that it “shall not return unto me void, but it shall accomplish that which I please” (Isa 55:11), and Jeremiah describes its force in terms no censor can domesticate: “Is not my word like as a fire? saith the LORD; and like a hammer that breaketh the rock in pieces?” (Jer 23:29). A single surviving leaf is a fragment of a hammer.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew pethach (H6608), an opening; Greek anakrino (G0350), to examine; Hebrew pattish (H6360), a hammer.

expand to see more

Hebrew 'or (H0216) — light; “The entrance of thy words giveth light”, Psalm 119:130.

Hebrew pethi (H6612) — simple, untaught; “it giveth understanding unto the simple”, Psalm 119:130.

Greek anakrino (G0350) — to examine, to sift; “and searched the scriptures daily”, Acts 17:11.

Hebrew pattish (H6360) — a hammer, a forge hammer; “and like a hammer that breaketh the rock in pieces”, Jeremiah 23:29.

Hebrew 'esh (H0784) — fire; “Is not my word like as a fire?”, Jeremiah 23:29.

Usage

"“and searched the scriptures daily” (Act 17:11) — the practice a suppressed Bible was meant to prevent."

"“it giveth understanding unto the simple” (Psa 119:130) — the whole argument for translation."

"“and like a hammer that breaketh the rock in pieces” (Jer 23:29) — what one surviving leaf is a fragment of."
